notes:
Here are the verse-by-verse notes for 1 Samuel 20:22–42, drawn from the pages I was able to search and read within the allowed sites.

---

## Verse 22

**v. 22 — “But if I say to the young man, ‘Look, the arrows are beyond you,’ then you must go, for the LORD has sent you away.”**

Jonathan continues laying out the pre-arranged signal. If he shoots the arrows beyond the lad and calls out accordingly, David is to understand that Saul's heart remains murderous and David must flee immediately. **Gill** notes that the arrows shot to a greater distance than where the lad stood indicated that David was to "depart directly, without staying to have any conversation with Jonathan, which would not be safe for either of them" — it was understood as God's providence directing him to leave. (URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-20.html)

**Trapp** captures the urgency with the Latin phrase *Fuge, fuge, cito, citius, citissime* — "flee, flee, quickly, more quickly, most quickly" — and adds that David must "shift for thyself, and so serve God's providence in such a way as he shall direct thee." (URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jtc/1-samuel-20.html)

**David Guzik** (Enduring Word, Pentecostal/charismatic tradition) remarks that the three-arrow signal would bring one of two messages: either Saul's heart had changed and there was safety, or Saul was still determined to kill David and "the LORD has sent you away." (URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-20/)

---

## Verse 23

**v. 23 — “And as for the matter you and I have discussed, the LORD is a witness between you and me forever.”**

**Gill** explains that the "matter" refers to the covenant they had made with each other, and that the LORD stands as "a witness of the covenant, and a revenger of those that should break it." The Targum (ancient Aramaic paraphrase) renders it the same way. (URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-20.html)

The **Pulpit Commentary** renders it: "As for the word that we have spoken, I and thou, behold, Jehovah is between me and thee forever." It notes that "the word was the bond and covenant by which they had pledged their truth to one another. Though separated, their love was to continue, and Jehovah was to be their eternal centre of union, and the witness to their covenant." (URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_samuel/20.htm)

**Trapp** reads it as a warning: "The mutual covenant, see that it be kept inviolable, or the Lord will require it." (URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jtc/1-samuel-20.html)

---

## Verse 24

**v. 24 — “So David hid in the field, and when the New Moon had come, the king sat down to eat.”**

**Guzik** notes that this was a special monthly feast for the high officials of state, with special sacrifices commanded in Numbers 28:11–15 for the new moon. David hid in the field as planned. (URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-20/)

**Ellicott** observes that the LXX paraphrases "sat down to eat" simply as "came to the table." He also notes that Saul's court carefully observed the new moon feast with solemn burnt offerings, sin offerings, and a state banquet at which David, as the king's son-in-law and a high-ranking army officer, was expected. (URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-20.html)

---

## Verse 25

**v. 25 — “He sat in his usual place by the wall, opposite Jonathan and beside Abner, but David's place was empty.”**

**Ellicott** discusses a textual difficulty with the phrase "and Jonathan arose." The LXX and some Hebrew manuscripts read differently. The explanation of the medieval Jewish commentators Abarbanel and Rashi (cited by Ellicott and Lange) is that Jonathan, seeing David's seat empty, arose and seated Abner next to Saul so the vacant place wouldn't be obvious. This reads the Hebrew verb as causative (Hiphil). (URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-20.html)

**Guzik** simply notes that David was expected at this feast and his absence was clearly noticed; the king sat in his customary seat by the wall. (URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-20/)

---

## Verse 26

**v. 26 — “Saul said nothing that day because he thought, 'Something has happened to David to make him ceremonially unclean—surely he is unclean.'”**

**Guzik** explains that ceremonial uncleanness would cause a person to miss such a feast (Leviticus 22:3–7). However, such uncleanness only lasted one day — therefore Saul's acceptance lasted only that first day. (URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-20/)

**Ellicott** adds that the plea of possible ceremonial uncleanness was "at once accepted as an excuse for absence" at Saul's court, underscoring how seriously these purity laws were observed at the royal table. (URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-20.html)

---

## Verse 27

**v. 27 — “But on the day after the New Moon, the second day, David's place was still empty, and Saul asked his son Jonathan, 'Why hasn't the son of Jesse come to the meal either yesterday or today?'”**

**Ellicott** says that David's continued absence on the second day "awoke Saul's suspicion," since no accident of ceremonial defilement would keep him away two consecutive days. (URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-20.html)

**Guzik** notes that Saul refers to David derisively as "the son of Jesse" — citing Meyer: "Speaking of him derisively as 'the son of Jesse,' thus accentuating his lowly birth, and ignoring the relationship that bound him to the royal family." (URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-20/)

---

## Verses 28–29

**vv. 28–29 — “Jonathan answered, 'David urgently requested my permission to go to Bethlehem, saying, "Please let me go, because our clan is holding a sacrifice in the city, and my brother has told me to be there…" That is why he did not come to the king's table.'”**

Jonathan gives the planned excuse. **Poole** (cited by Guzik) comments: "It seems probable that he went first to Bethlehem, as he bade Jonathan to tell his father … and thence returned to the field, when the occasion required; else we must charge him with a downright lie, which ought not to be imagined (without any apparent cause) concerning so good a man." (URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-20/)

**Ellicott** notes that the LXX has "my brothers" (plural) instead of "my brother," apparently not understanding why the singular "brother" would summon David since Jesse was still alive. Dean Payne Smith suggests the "brother" is the eldest brother, acting as convener of the absent family member. (URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-20.html)

**Ellicott** also notes that the excuse was "feigned" — David did not actually plan to attend the Bethlehem sacrifice — and that "the morality of this request of David is by no means sanctioned by the compiler of the history; he simply relates the story." (URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-20.html)

---

## Verse 30

**v. 30 — “Then Saul's anger burned against Jonathan, and he said to him, 'You son of a perverse and rebellious woman! Do I not know that you have chosen the son of Jesse to your own shame and to the disgrace of the mother who bore you?'”**

**Guzik**: "Jonathan knew from this response that Saul's heart was settled on evil against David. If Saul's heart was different towards David, he might have been disappointed but not furious." (URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-20/)

**Ellicott** offers an alternative translation: the Hebrew word *naăvath* (rendered "perverse") is probably an abstract noun rather than a feminine adjective. The phrase then means "Thou son of perversity of rebellion" — a Hebraism for "a man of perverse and refractory nature." This, Ellicott argues, "avoids the extreme improbability that Saul insulted his own wife, Jonathan's mother, which … contradicts the Hebrew family spirit." The phrase about "the confusion of thy mother's nakedness" is "simply an Oriental mode of saying, 'she will feel ashamed at having brought such a son into the world.'" (URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-20.html)

---

## Verse 31

**v. 31 — “For as long as the son of Jesse lives on this earth, neither you nor your kingship shall be established. Now send for him and bring him to me, for he must surely die!”**

**Guzik** notes: "Certainly, this was Saul's intention, despite his previous oath (As the LORD lives, he shall not be killed, 1 Samuel 19:6). Despite Saul's intentions, David would not die at the hands of Saul or any other enemy. Man proposes, but God disposes." (URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-20/)

**Ellicott** says Saul "betrays his fell purpose" with the command "Send and fetch him unto me" — the murder had been pre-arranged to occur at the feast: "Doubtless those rough soldier chiefs sitting round the royal table would be ready at any moment to carry into effect their master's savage behest." (URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-20.html)

---

## Verse 32

**v. 32 — “'Why must he be put to death?' Jonathan replied. 'What has he done?'”**

**Guzik**: "Jonathan responded by defending not only David but right in this cause. His support of David wasn't blind support; it was based on what was right before the LORD." (URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-20/)

**Meyer** (cited by Guzik) says, "Jonathan made one vain attempt to reason with the furious monarch; he might as well have tried to arrest the swelling of Jordan in the time of flood." (URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-20/)

**Ellicott**: "Jonathan, remembering the effect of his quiet, earnest remonstrance on a previous occasion, again tried to deprecate his father's unreasoning jealous anger, but this time to no purpose." (URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-20.html)

---

## Verse 33

**v. 33 — “Then Saul hurled his spear at Jonathan to kill him; so Jonathan knew that his father was determined to kill David.”**

**Guzik**: "This shows how deep Saul's hatred of David was — he would kill his own son for siding with David." (URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-20/)

**Ellicott** says a "paroxysm of madness seized Saul, and he grasped the long spear leaning by his side, and with hate and fury in his eye raised the great war weapon to strike down his son." (URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-20.html)

**Jamieson-Fausset-Brown** concisely states: "Jonathan knew that it was determined of his father to slay David." (URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/1_samuel/20.htm)

---

## Verse 34

**v. 34 — “Jonathan got up from the table in fierce anger and did not eat any food that second day of the month, for he was grieved by his father's shameful treatment of David.”**

**Guzik** simply notes Jonathan arose in fierce anger, grieved for David because his father had treated him shamefully. (URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-20/)

**Ellicott** parses Jonathan's "fierce anger" as stirred by two things: first, "the terrible insult offered him, the prince and heir to the throne, before the assembled great ones of Israel" with the great spear uplifted to strike; and second, "the determined and relentless enmity of Saul against David, of whose stainless integrity and perfect loyalty Jonathan was firmly convinced. The bitter wrong done to David his friend no doubt affected Jonathan most." (URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-20.html)

---

## Verse 35

**v. 35 — “In the morning Jonathan went out to the field for the appointment with David, and a small boy was with him.”**

The **Pulpit Commentary** notes that Jonathan went "not at the time, but 'to the place' appointed," taking "a little lad, as less likely to suspect a reason." (URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_samuel/20.htm)

**Ellicott**: "This meeting between the friends is not described at any length; all was done as had been pre-arranged, and, alas! everything had come to pass as David in his sad foresight had expected." (URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-20.html)

---

## Verses 36–38

**vv. 36–38 — The arrow signal executed: Jonathan shoots an arrow beyond the boy, calls out “Isn't the arrow beyond you?” and cries “Hurry! Make haste! Do not delay!”**

**Jamieson-Fausset-Brown**: "The direction given aloud to the attendant was the signal preconcerted with David. It implied danger." (URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/1_samuel/20.htm)

The **Pulpit Commentary** notes that Jonathan shoots one arrow beyond him — the written text (Kethib) has the singular "arrow," not "arrows" — and "to keep the boy's attention engaged he gives him hurried commands — Make speed, haste, stay not." (URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_samuel/20.htm)

**Guzik**: "It took courage for Jonathan to communicate with David, even secretly — because he knew that if his father became aware of it, he would focus his murderous rage against Jonathan again." He also applies it devotionally, citing Meyer: "But there is something still nobler — when one dares in any company to avow his loyalty to the Lord Jesus. Like David, he is now in obscurity and disrepute … These are days when to stand up for anything more than mere conventional religion must cost something." (URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-20/)

---

## Verse 39

**v. 39 — “But the boy did not know anything; only Jonathan and David knew the arrangement.”**

**Guzik**: "A small thing — the signal of a single arrow — told David his whole life was changed. He would no longer be welcome at the palace. He would no longer be welcome among the army of Israel. He could no longer go home. David was now a fugitive on the run from an angry, jealous king determined to destroy him." He adds a practical application: "Sometimes our life turns on a small thing … It often does not seem fair that so much in life should turn on small moments, but a lifetime is made of nothing but many small moments." (URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-20/)

---

## Verse 40

**v. 40 — “Then Jonathan gave his equipment to the boy and said, 'Go, take it back to the city.'”**

The **Pulpit Commentary**: "To get rid of the boy Jonathan sends him home with his bow and arrows." (URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_samuel/20.htm)

**Trapp** adds: "The lad he sent away, that David and he might talk together the more freely; for he knew that little pitchers also have ears." (URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jtc/1-samuel-20.html)

---

## Verse 41

**v. 41 — “When the young man had gone, David got up from the south side of the stone, fell facedown, and bowed three times. Then he and Jonathan kissed each other and wept together—though David wept more.”**

**Ellicott** discusses the difficult Hebrew phrase *mêêtzel hannegev*, rendered "out of a place toward the south." He notes that the Chaldee reads "from the stone of the sign (or the stone Atha) which is on the south"; the LXX (Vatican MS) reads "from the Argab"; the Alexandrian MS reads "from sleep." The versions "fail altogether to understand" the original. He suggests David rose from the south side of the rock where he had been concealed. (URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-20.html)

**Jamieson-Fausset-Brown**: "David … fell on his face to the ground, and bowed three times — a token of homage to the prince's rank; but on a close approach, every other consideration was sunk in the full flow of the purest brotherly affection." (URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/1_samuel/20.htm)

**Ellicott**, citing Josephus, explains David's bowing: "He did obeisance, and called him the saviour of his life." (URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-20.html)

On "until David exceeded," **Ellicott** gives Dean Payne Smith's interpretation: the phrase "apparently signifies either simply that while Jonathan wept bitterly at the parting, David wept still more, or else that 'David broke down,' that is, 'was completely mastered by his grief.'" The LXX rendering is unintelligible at this point — "until a (or the) great consummation." (URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-20.html)

The **Pulpit Commentary** likewise says "until David exceeded" means David "broke down, and was completely mastered by his grief." (URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_samuel/20.htm)

**Whedon** (Methodist): "Until David exceeded — Surpassed Jonathan in the exhibition of his grief, and wept aloud over his sorrows; for, says Bishop Patrick, he was now about to become an exile from his friends, his wife, his kindred, the people of God, and all the solemnities of sacred worship." (URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/1-samuel-20.html)

**Guzik** captures the poignancy: "David and Jonathan loved each other and had a strong bond of friendship. Jonathan and David probably envisioned working together, as partners, as friends … But now all that was gone because David couldn't stay and Jonathan couldn't go, so they wept together." He cites Meyer: "Behind you is the sunny morning, before you a lowering sky; behind you the blessed enjoyment of friendship, wife, home, royal favor, and popular adulation, before you an outcast's life." (URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-20/)

**Trapp** quotes a Greek proverb: "The better any one is, the more apt to weep. But David indeed had the greater reason in many regards." (URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jtc/1-samuel-20.html)

---

## Verse 42

**v. 42 — “And Jonathan said to David, 'Go in peace, for the two of us have sworn in the name of the LORD, saying, "May the LORD be a witness between you and me, and between your descendants and mine forever."' Then David got up and departed, and Jonathan went back into the city.”**

**Ellicott** says of "Go in peace": "The abruptness of the closing words is most natural, and accords with the evident deep emotion of the speaker. David's heart was too full to reply to his friend's words; blinded with tears, he seems to have hurried away speechless." (URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-20.html)

The **biblehub.com** margin rendering (Cambridge Bible for Schools and Colleges) suggests an *aposiopesis* (a broken-off sentence) corresponding to Jonathan's deep emotion: "That which we have sworn, etc. — remember!" (URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_samuel/20-42.htm)

**Gill**: "Go in peace … in peace of mind, committing himself, his family, and affairs, to the providence of God, who would take care of him, and keep him in safety from the evil designs of Saul." (URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-20.html)

**Trapp** notes the broken-speech reading: "Some read it, What things soever we have sworn, …, making it to be an elliptical broken speech: as it is usual with those that are in heaviness to utter half sentences." (URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jtc/1-samuel-20.html)

**Guzik** applies it: "Jonathan knew he might never see David again. In fact, David and Jonathan will only meet once more, shortly before Jonathan's death. Yet as David now left for a life of hiding and danger, Jonathan could send David away in peace because they both agreed to honor each other not only in life, but also to honor each other's families beyond their own lifetimes." He then reflects on the theological point that this bleak road was God's path for David — to teach him dependence on God alone: "If God would put David in a place where people must depend on him, God must teach David to depend upon Him alone. Not himself, not Saul, not Jonathan, not anyone except God." He quotes Alan Redpath: "Let God empty you out that He may save you from becoming spiritually stale, and lead you ever onward … A throne is God's purpose for you; a cross is God's path for you; faith is God's plan for you." (URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-20/)

The **Church Pulpit Commentary** (Anglican) draws out the theme of parting: "There are partings in every life … We are closely bound to each other by the strong bonds of circumstances one moment, and the next we are severed and each goes on his way to strive or to suffer … alone." But for David and Jonathan, "theirs had been no light and trifling friendship … but a serious, manly, steadfast love, rooted in a common faith and held together by a common object animating their lives; and therefore the one could say to the other, 'Go in peace, forasmuch as we have sworn both of us in the name of the Lord.'" (URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cpc/1-samuel-20.html)

---

## Protestant Traditions: Differences in Emphasis

On this narrative passage, Protestant traditions largely agree on the historical-grammatical meaning. The differences appear in application and theological emphasis:

**Reformed / The Gospel Coalition (Paul Tripp):** Emphasises the relational and redemptive dimension — Jonathan's selfless yielding of his claim to the throne points to a gospel pattern of dying to self for the good of another. (URL: https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/sermon/1-samuel-20-david-and-jonathan/)

**Reformed / Desiring God (John Piper's ministry):** Focuses on Jonathan as "the glory of humbly yielding power." The article notes that Jonathan "did not consider the throne a thing to be grasped, but for the sake of God he made himself nothing and became a Christ-like servant," explicitly connecting Jonathan to Philippians 2:5–11. (URL: https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/jonathan-the-glory-of-humbly-yielding-power)

**Baptist / Grace to You (John MacArthur):** In his sermon "Jonathan: The Man Who Would Not Be King," MacArthur traces the whole story of Saul's disobedience and replacement, emphasising Jonathan's fearless faith ("the LORD is not restrained to save by many or by few," 1 Sam 14:6) and his willing relinquishment of the throne. He underscores Jonathan as an unlikely hero precisely because he submitted to God's will rather than grasping for power. (URL: https://www.gty.org/sermons/80-391/jonathan-the-man-who-would-not-be-king)

**Pentecostal/Charismatic (David Guzik, Enduring Word):** Guzik's commentary draws strong practical and devotional applications — the "bleak road" as God's school of dependence, the danger of small moments that pivot a life, and the importance of loyalty to Christ when it costs. He quotes Alan Redpath and F.B. Meyer extensively for devotional warmth. (URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-20/)

**Methodist/Wesleyan (Whedon):** Whedon's notes focus on the moral and emotional dimensions — Jonathan's righteous indignation, David's deeper grief as the one losing everything, and the appeal to Bishop Patrick regarding the pain of exile from the means of grace and sacred worship. (URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/1-samuel-20.html)

**Anglican (Church Pulpit Commentary):** Draws out the universal experience of parting in every life, and finds comfort in the fact that their friendship was "rooted in a common faith" — a bond that survives separation. (URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cpc/1-samuel-20.html)

**Spurgeon (Reformed Baptist):** In his sermon "A Word for the Persecuted" on 1 Samuel 20:10, Spurgeon applies the question "What if thy father answer thee roughly?" to new believers facing family opposition: "Will they follow the Lord through evil report? … Remember that this supposition is a very likely one." He encourages steadfastness when dearest friends turn hostile. (URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/1-samuel-20.html)
